cues: P.S.C.I. 1104. Understanding Political Controversy. The
Condensed Audito Guide.
This is the whole course in about 35 minutes. It is built to be
listened to more than once.
So do not worry about catching everything the first time. Play
it on the walk to class.
Play it the night before a quiz. A note on how this is
organized.
The course has 14 concepts and 7 debates. The concepts are the
machinery. The debates
are worked examples. I will give you the machinery first.
In the order Professor Troustine teaches it. And then run
through the 7 debates quickly at the end.
One more thing before we start. When I describe a figure from
the written guide.
I will describe what it shows in words. You do not need to be
looking at anything.
Here is the entire course in one sentence. Somebody claims that
X causes Y.
Should you believe them? That is it. That is the only question.
Every reading on the syllabus is a version of it.
Thomas Frank claims that cultural politics causes working class
whites to vote Republican.
Michael Bloomberg claims that stop and frisk is not racial
profiling.
Malcolm Gladwell claims that policing caused crime to fall in
New York.
In every case, somebody has made a causal claim and your job is
to figure out whether the evidence
supports it. Now, here is the thing that makes this class work.
Professor Troustine does not just assign the claim. She assigns
the claim and then she assigns a scholar
who tested it. Frank is paired with Bartels. Bloomberg is paired
with Bertrand and Molinathan.
Gladwell is paired with Levitt. The pairing is the lesson. When
you read the journalism,
ask yourself, what evidence would settle this? When you read the
scholar, ask yourself,
what technique did they use to get it? If you can do those two
things, you will pass this class.
Let us start with what research actually is. Science is not a
pile of facts. It is a loop.
You have a hunch about why something happens. You turn that
hunch into a prediction. You collect
evidence. You find out whether you were right. The part that
makes it science is that the prediction
has to be able to lose. If no possible evidence could prove you
wrong, you are not doing science.
That property has a name. It is called falsifiability. Remember
that word. Here is the vocabulary.
A theory is a general explanation of why X causes Y. It has to
apply beyond the one case in front of you.
For example, voting is partly social because people vote to
avoid looking like a shirker.
A hypothesis is one specific, testable prediction that follows
from the theory. It has to name two
variables and a direction. For example, households told that
their neighbors will see their turnout record
will vote at higher rates than households that are not told.
Notice the shape of that. As X increases,
Y increases or decreases across some unit of analysis. That is
the template. Two variables,
a direction, a unit, and a way to lose. If you were asked to
write a hypothesis on an exam,
use that template. Two more terms. The independent variable,
which we call X, is the proposed cause.
The dependent variable, Y, is the defect. Y depends on X. That
is how you remember which is which.
And the null hypothesis is the claim that there is no
relationship at all between X and Y.
That matters more than it sounds. Because the null is what you
actually test. We will come back to it.
Four ways students lose points on hypothesis questions.
1. No validation. Asking why do people vote. And then only
studying voters.
2. Writing a definition instead of a claim. Partisans are loyal
to their party. That is not a hypothesis.
That is what partisan means. 3. Writing about a single case.
Trump won because of the economy.
There is nothing to compare it to. 4. No direction. Education is
related to turn out does not say which
way. The very first reading of the semester is Fisman, Gelman,
and Stephenson, on what they call
the statistics that come out of nowhere. They trace famous
numbers back to their sources and find that
most of them have no source at all. Their examples are quiz
-friendly, so learn them.
You lose 80% of your body heat through your head. This comes
from a 1950s military study,
where the subjects were wearing arctic suits that covered
everything except the head.
The real figure is about 10%. Bribery costs $1 trillion a year.
That is the midpoint of a range
that ran from $600 billion to $1.7 trillion. Taking the
midpoint, deletes the uncertainty,
which was the most honest part of the estimate. Corruption costs
$2.6 trillion. That one traces
back to a single bullet point in an advocacy brief that cited no
source, and then got repeated by the
heads of the United Nations and the OECD. And Dan Keel claiming
that 70% of the world's lawyers are
American. The real share is 25 to 35%. They give you four rules.
First, trace the number to the
original source, not to whoever cited it. Studies have shown,
and it has been estimated, are red flags.
Second, watch for what they call statistics laundering. A shaky
figure gets repeated by a
respectable body, and then everybody cites the respectable body.
Third, a Harvard professor's guess
is not a Harvard estimate. Fourth, beware the broken telephone
effect. Ranges collapse into single
points. Caveats fall off. Narrow findings get generalized. Now
the most important practical
skill in this course. Measurement. You cannot test a claim about
the working class until you say exactly
who counts. Here is the latter. A concept is the abstract idea.
Democracy. Ideology. The working class.
Discrimination. A conceptual definition is what you mean by that
idea. In words, the working class is
people whose income depends on wages rather than on assets or
credentials. An operational definition is
the exact recipe for measuring it, specific enough that a
stranger following it would produce the same
numbers. The working class is white respondents with no four
-year college degree. That last step is
where arguments are won and lost. Two quality checks on any
measure. Validity asks. Are you
measuring the thing you claim to be measuring? Reliability asks.
Does the same procedure give the
same answer every time? Picture four dartboards. On the first,
the darts are clustered tightly on the
bullseye. That is valid and reliable. On the second, the darts
are clustered tightly, but up in the top
right corner, nowhere near the center. That is reliable but not
valid, and it is the dangerous one. A measure
can be perfectly consistent and perfectly wrong. On the third
dartboard the darts are scattered all around
the bullseye. That is valid but not reliable. Right on average,
but noisy. On the fourth,
they are scattered and off center. That is neither. Here is why
the second dartboard matters.
Self-reported turnout is reliable. People answer the same way
every time. It is also invalid,
because people over-report whether they voted, and more data
never fixes a validity problem.
That is the sentence to remember. Levels of measurement,
quickly. Nominal variables name categories
with no order. Party. Religion. State. Ordinal variables rank
categories but the gaps between
them are not equal. Strongly the greed down to strongly
disagree. Interval or ratio-bow variables
are real numbers with equal gaps. Turnout percentage. Income.
Age. The classic quiz trap here. You cannot
take a mean of a nominal variable. The average religion is
nonsense. Ordinal variables get a median,
not a mean, because the distance from agree to strongly agree is
not a known quantity.
Now watch measurement decide an entire political argument.
Thomas Frank argues that working-class
whites have abandoned the Democrats because culture outweighs
economics. His evidence includes the fact
that the poorest county in America voted for Bush by more than
75 percent. Larry Bartles asks the
measurement question. Who exactly is the working class? And when
he changes the operational definition,
the answer flips. Here are the numbers. Take the cumulative
change in the Democratic share of the
two-party presidential vote from 1952 to 2004. Among all white
voters with no college degree,
the Democrats lost 5.9 points. That looks like Frank is right.
But split it by region. In the South,
the Democrats lost 19.7 points. Outside the South, they lost 1.0
points. 1 point. In 52 years,
across 14 elections, essentially nothing happened outside the
South, and Southern realignment was
about race, not about the culture war. Now change the definition
of working class from education to
income. Among white voters in the bottom third by income, the
Democrats gained 4.5 points. The
poorest white voters moved toward the Democrats, not away. Same
concept. Three operational definitions.
Three different answers. And there is a validity problem with
Frank's definition on its face.
In 2004, 40 percent of white voters without a college degree had
family incomes over $60,000,
and more than half described themselves as middle class. No
college degree is simply not a good
measure of working class. Two more numbers worth having. Bush's
margin among the poorest third of
white non-college voters in 2004 was under 2 percentage points.
And in that same year, abortion
ranked 13th out of 15 issues in terms of how much weight non
-college whites gave it. Also file away
Patrick Ruffina's update. In 1996, Clinton won the lowest-income
voters by 31 points while Dole won the
highest earners by 16. That is a 47-point spread across the
income scale. By 2020, that spread had
collapsed to about 8 points. Income barely divides the American
electorate anymore.
A short unit on describing a variable, because it shows up on
quizzes.
Three measures of the middle. The mode is the most common value,
and it is the only average that
works for nominal variables. The median is the middle case when
you line them up, and it ignores extremes.
The mean is the arithmetic average, and it gets dragged toward
outliers. Two measures of spread.
The range is highest minus lowest, which is crude and hostage to
one weird case.
The standard divination is the typical distance of a case from
the mean.
And skew. A distribution is skewed when it has a long tail on
one side. Here is the rule.
The mean always sits toward the tail. So in a right skewed
distribution, like income,
the order from left to right is mode, then median, then mean. A
handful of very rich people pull the mean
far above the median. That is exactly why average income
flatters and median income describes.
One more concept that costs students a lot of points. The
ecological fallacy. That is inferring
something about individuals from data about groups. Poor
counties voted for Bush. Therefore poor people
voted for Bush. That does not follow. The unit of analysis was
the county, not the person. This is
the error in Frank's rent state map, and, as we will see, in the
chocolate study.
This is the single most testable thing in the course. So if you
remember one segment of this
recording, make it this one. Kelset and Witten give you four
questions to run any causal claim
through. Take them in order. Herbal 1. Is there a credible
causal mechanism connecting X to Y?
Not just a correlation. A story about how X would actually
produce Y.
Herbal 2. Can we rule out the possibility that Y causes X? That
is reverse causation.
Hurdle 3. Is there actually co-varidation between X and Y? Do
they move together at all?
Hurdle 4. Have we controlled for all the confounding variables Z
that might make the relationship
spurious? Answer each one yes, no, or maybe, one confident no
kills the claim. And here is the
crucial framing. You never prove causation. You accumulate
confidence. Now notice something.
Hurdle 3. Co-varidation is the easy one. It is also the only one
most people ever check.
A correlation clears hurdle 3 and tells you nothing about the
other three.
Let me give you the flagship example. In 2012, Frank Messoli
published a paper in the New England
Journal of Medicine correlating national chocolate consumption
with Nobel Prizes per capita across
23 countries. The correlation was R equals 0.79, with a p-value
under 0.0001. That is a strong,
statistically significant, completely real correlation. Now run
the hurdles.
Mechanism. There is no plausible story about national chocolate
consumption producing Nobel laureates.
Reverse causation. Live and obvious. Rich, well-educated
countries buy more expensive chocolate.
Confounders. Everyone you can name is uncontrolled. Wealth.
Education. Research funding. Being in
Northern Europe. And the unit of analysis is the country, so it
also commits the ecological fallacy.
Not one laureate's diet was ever observed. Messoli wrote it as a
joke. It is on your syllabus because
the joke keeps getting taken seriously. Now, what does the word
cause actually mean?
Buenodamasquita and Fowler define it with a counterfactual. X
caused Y for a case if Y would
have been different had X been different, with everything else
held fixed. That definition creates
the central problem of the entire field. For each case there are
two potential outcomes. The outcome
if treated, and the outcome if not treated. The causal effect is
the difference between them,
but you only ever get to observe one of the two. The
counterfactual is never seen.
That is called the fundamental problem of causal inference, and
it is worth knowing by name.
Its consequence is that a causal effect is never measured
directly. It is always inferred
by finding a believable stand-in for the missing counterfactual.
That stand-in is your control
group. Every method in this course is a scheme for building a
credible control group.
One more thing here, because people forget it. Correlation does
not imply causation,
but also, causation does not require correlation. A real causal
effect can show zero correlation if
it runs in opposite directions for different groups, or if
people compensate for it.
There are four things a correlation between X and Y can mean,
and you should be able to tell
them apart. 1. X causes Y. That is the claim. 2. Y causes X.
An arrow pointing backwards.
Hurdle 2 fails. 3. Some third variable Z causes both X and Y.
Picture Z sitting above,
with arrows running down to X on the left and Y on the right,
and no arrow between X and Y at all.
That is a spurious relationship. Hurdle 4 fails. 4. X causes Y
through some middle variable M.
X, then M, then Y in a chain. That is called mediation, and it
is still causal. It explains the
relationship rather than destroying it. Here is the distinction
that shows up on exams. A variable
that comes before X and causes both X and Y is called an
antecedent variable, and it makes the
relationship spurious. A variable that sits between X and Y and
transmits the defect is called an
intervening variable, and it explains the mechanism. The
diagrams look similar. The verdicts are opposite.
Two kinds of validity in research design, and you need both
words.
Internal validity asks whether the relationship you found inside
your study is really causal.
External validity asks whether it generalizes to other people,
other places, other times.
Now the distinction that comes up every single semester. Random
assignment is not the same thing
as random sampling. Random sampling decides who is in your
study. It buys external validity,
because your sample looks like the population. Random assignment
decides who gets the treatment.
It buys internal validity, because the treatment and control
groups are equivalent before you do
anything. A national survey has the first and not the second. A
lab experiment on 60 undergraduates has
the second and not the first. Know which is which. Threats to
internal validity. There is a standard list,
and it is very quizable. History, meaning something else
happened between the protest and the postist.
Maturation, meaning subjects changed on their own over time.
Testing, meaning taking the protest itself
changed the postist. Instrumentation, meaning the measuring
device drifted. Regression to the mean,
meaning extreme cases drift back toward average all by
themselves. Selection bias, meaning the groups
differed before the treatment. Attrition, meaning people dropped
out non-randomly. Demand effects,
sometimes called the Hawthorne effect, meaning subjects behave
differently because they knew they were
being watched. And diffusion, meaning the control group got the
treatment anyway. Of that list,
selection bias is the big one. It is the single largest threat
in observational research.
Why do experiments work? One reason, and it is worth stating
precisely.
Randomization balances confounders that you never thought of.
Statistical controls can only adjust for
variables you measured. Random assignment balances everything at
once. On average, observed and
unobserved, the asymmetry is the whole argument for experiments.
The anatomy is simple. Take a subject
pool. Randomly assign each subject to treatment or control.
Apply the treatment to one group and not
another. Compare the outcomes. The difference is the causal
effect. And the check that randomization
worked is called a balance table, where you compare the groups
on background characteristics
before the treatment. If a study skips the balance table, ask
why. Now the two experiments you will
definitely be tested on. First, Gerber, Green and Larimer, 2008,
Social Pressure and Voter Turnout,
a field experiment on 180,002 households, before the August 2006
Michigan primary, they sent four
different mailings. The control group, which got no mail, voted
at 29.7%. The civic duty mailing,
which just said do your duty and vote, produced 31.5%, a lift of
1.8 points. The Hawthorne mailing,
which told households they were being studied, produced 32.2%, a
lift of 2.5. The self-mailing,
which showed the household its own voting record, produced 34
.5%, a lift of 4.9. And the neighbor's
mailing, which showed the household its neighbor's voting
records and promise to send an updated
version after the election, produced 37.8%, a lift of 8.1
points. Now, why four treatments instead of
one? Because a single mailer would only show that mail works.
This is a dosage design, and it identifies
the mechanism. Each step adds one ingredient, and the jump tells
you what that ingredient is worth.
Priming civic duty barely moves anybody. Beating observed moves
them more. Seeing your own record
moves them more still. Threatening to show the neighbors nearly
doubles that again. Turnout is
not driven by information. It is driven by beating scene. For
context, before the study, a single mailing
typically move turnout by less than one percentage point. 8.1
points is enormous, and it cost $1.93
per additional vote, against roughly $20 per vote for door-to
-door canvassing.
Second experiment. Burkhand and Malenathan, 2004. Are Emily and
Greg more employable than
Lakisha and Jamal? They sent about 5,000 resumes to more than 1
,300 job advertisements in Boston
and Chicago. The resumes were identical in every respect except
the name at the top, which was
randomly assigned to sound either white or African-American.
Resumes with white-sounding names
got a callback 9.65% of the time. Resumes with African-American
-sounding names got a callback 6.45%
of the time. That is a gap of 3.2 percentage points, which means
white names got 50% more callbacks.
The authors estimate the gap is worth about eight additional
years of experience.
Here is the design point. In any observational study of hiring,
employers see more about applicants
than researchers do, so any observed gap might be something
unmeasured. Randomly assigning the name
to an otherwise identical resume removes that possibility
completely. There is nothing left
that could differ except the name. And notice one more finding,
because it is counterintuitive.
They also varied resume quality. Improving the resume raised
callbacks for white names by 2.29 points,
from 8.50% to 10.79. For African-American names it raised
callbacks by only 0.51 points,
from 6.19 to 6.70, which was not statistically significant. The
gap gets wider as qualifications
improve, not narrower. Most political questions cannot be
randomized. You cannot assign somebody
a race, a region, or an income. So what do you do? You use
controlled comparison. Split the sample by
the suspected confounder Z, and look at the relationship between
X and Y inside each slice.
Three things can happen. If the relationship holds inside every
slice, then Z was not doing the work,
and X survives. If the relationship disappears in every slice,
it was spurious. And if the relationship
is strong in one slice and absent in another, you have an
interaction. Meaning X matters, but only under
certain conditions. Bartle's region analysis is exactly this.
Uncontrolled, white non-college voters
shifted 5.9 points Republican. Control for region. And it is 19
.7 in the south and 1.0 outside it.
The confounder was doing almost all of the work. But here is the
permanent limit. And it is the
standard critique to deploy on any exam question about survey
-based causal claims. You can only control
for variables you measured and thought of. Randomization
balances the ones you did not.
Now, Lili and Nagler are on the syllabus for a subtler reason.
They show you when to control and
when not to. Two questions that sound identical and are not.
First, are poor people underrepresented
among voters? For that, do not control for anything. Just
compare shares. Second, is a poor person less
likely to vote than an otherwise identical richer person? For
that you must control, because income rises
with age and young people vote less. Their tool for the first
question is called the representativeness
ratio. Take a group's share of actual voters and divide it by
that group's share of the citizen voting
age population. 1.0 means proportional. Above 1 means
overrepresented. Below 1 means underrepresented.
The headline result is that nothing moved. The bottom fifth of
the income distribution had a
representativeness ratio of 0.79 in 1972 and 0.79 in
2008. 36 years of exploding economic inequality,
and the income bias and turnout was identical at both ends. The
top fifth went from 1.23 to 1.17,
which is actually slightly less overrepresented. Where things
did change was race. Black voters went from
0.82 to 1.02, from underrepresented to rough parity. And one
more finding worth having, because it is a
great example of a measurement trap. Turnout has not declined.
Measured against citizens, it ranged from
58.4% to 65.5% with no trend. The famous decline everybody cites
is a denominator artifact. Non-citizens
grew from under 2% of the voting age population in 1972 to 8.4%
in 2008. Count them in the denominator,
and turnout looks like it is falling when it is not. Now
surveys. First, drawing a sample.
The population is everyone you want to describe. The sample is
the part you actually examine.
The sampling frame is the list you actually draw from, and the
gap between the frame and the
population is where coverage error lives. A parameter is the
true number in the population,
fixed and unknown. A statistic is the number in your sample,
known and different every time you
draw a new sample. Statistics estimate parameters. A simple
random sample of size N is chosen so that
every set of N individuals in the population has an equal chance
of being the sample. Note that
wording carefully. Every individual having an equal chance is
necessary, but not sufficient.
Two bad designs you must be able to name. A convenient sample
takes whoever is easy to reach.
A voluntary response sample lets people select themselves in,
like a call-in poll or an often
web survey, and it over-represents people with strong, usually
negative opinions.
Now the crucial distinction. Bias versus variability. Bias means
being consistently off-target,
and the only fix is a better design. Variability means being
scattered, and the fix is a bigger sample,
same dartboard picture as before. The margin of error. Quick
rule. It is approximately one divided by the
square root of N. A sample of a thousand gives you about plus or
minus three points. Four hundred gives
you about plus or minus five. To cut the margin of error in half
you need four times the sample.
That is why almost every national poll is between 800 and 1500
people. Pass that you pay a lot for very
little. Two things that trip students up. The size of the
population does not matter, as long as the
population is at least about 100 times the sample. 1500 people
is just as good for Nashville as for the
entire United States. And second, that margin of error covers
random sampling error only.
The example to have ready is the Literary Digest poll of 1936.
They mailed out 10 million ballots and
got 2.4 million back, and confidently predicted that Landon
would beat Roosevelt. Roosevelt won in
a landslide. Their sample came from car registrations, telephone
books and magazine subscribers, all of which
meant affluent in 1936. That is coverage error. And respondents
chose whether to mail it back.
That is voluntary response. Gallup used a far smaller but better
design sample and got it right.
A huge sample cannot fix a biased design. This unit has one
idea. The reported margin of error is the
smallest error in a poll. Here is what the margin of error does
not cover. Coverage error, where whole
groups are missing from the frame. None response, where the
people you selected cannot be reached or
refuse, which is the dominant problem today. Response bias,
where people misreport because of social
desirability or memory. Question wording and question order.
Adjustment error, meaning the pollster's waiting
decisions. And likely voter modeling, meaning who the pollster
thinks will actually show up. None of those
shrink when you interview more people. Nate Cohn ran a beautiful
natural experiment on this in 2016.
He took a single Florida poll of 867 likely voters and gave the
identical raw interviews to four outside
pollsters. Same data, same respondents. Hence Cohn-Berland got
Clinton plus four. Charles Franklin
got Clinton plus three. Echelon Insights got Clinton plus one.
The New York Times upshot and Siena got
Clinton plus one. And a Stanford. Columbia and Microsoft team
got Trump plus one. That is a five-point
spread with zero difference in sampling. All of it came from two
judgment calls, how to weight the
sample and who counts as a likely voter. Their implied
electorates differed too. The white share
ranged from 65 to 70 percent, and the partisan balance ran from
Democrats plus five to Republicans
plus one. Cohn's conclusion is quotable. The reported margin of
error, he wrote, does not even come close
to capturing total survey error. Joshua Clinton made the same
point differently in 2024. He took one
survey and applied 16 defensible waiting schemes to it. The
results ranged from Harris plus 3.8 to Harris
plus 9.4, nearly six points, from waiting alone. And here is the
number that explains why waiting matters
so much. Only about five out of every hundred contacted
registered voters respond to a survey at
all. Waiting is not a technical detail bolted on at the end. It
is doing most of the work. The
practical advice from these readings. Average many polls rather
than trusting one. But know the limit.
Averaging cancels random noise. It does not cancel house
effects. If every pollster misses cell phone
only households the same way, the average is just as wrong. Now
the statistics section, and I am going to
keep this concrete. The normal curve, symmetric, bell-shaped,
defined entirely by its mean and its
standard divination. The row to memorize is 68, 95, 99.7. About
68% of cases fall within one standard
divination of the mean. About 95% within two. About 99.7% within
three. A z-score converts any value onto
that scale. Z equals the value minus the mean divided by the
standard divination. A z of two
means two standard divinations above average. Which puts you in
roughly the top two and a half percent.
Why does any of this matter? Because of the sampling
distribution. That is not the distribution of your
data. It is the distribution of the statistic across all the
samples you could have drawn.
It is normal, and it is centered on the true parameter. Its
standard divination has a special name,
the standard error, which measures how much your estimate would
bounce around from sample to sample.
Bigger sample, smaller standard error. Now, confidence
intervals. The formula is your estimate,
plus or minus 1.96 times the standard error for 95% confidence.
Here is the interpretation students
get wrong, so listen carefully. A 95% confidence interval does
not mean there is a 95% chance the
true value is inside this particular interval. The true value is
fixed. It is either in there or it is
not. What is 95% is the procedure. If you did this over and
over, 19 times out of 20 you would capture
the truth. Picture 20 horizontal lines stacked up, each one in
interval from a different sample,
with a vertical line running through them marking the truth. 19
of the 20 cross that vertical line.
1 misses. That is the 95%. Hypothesis testing in 4 steps. 1.
State the null hypothesis,
that there is no relationship between X and Y. 2. Assume it is
true. 3. Ask, if the null were true,
how likely is a relationship at least this big just from
sampling luck? That probability is the P value.
4. If P is less than .05, reject the null, and call the result
statistically significant.
Otherwise, you fail to reject it. And note that phrasing. You
never accept the null. You fail to
reject it. Two kinds of error. A type 1 error is a false
positive. You announce a relationship that
is not there. The .05 threshold caps that risk at 5%. A type 2
error is a false negative. You miss a
real relationship, usually because your sample was too small.
Now the three things that cost the most
points on this topic. First, statistically significant does not
mean important. With a big enough sample,
a trivial difference clears any threshold. With 300,000 cases, a
tenth of a point is significant and
means nothing. Second, small samples hide real effects. Failing
to reject the null is not evidence
that there is no relationship. Third, and most important,
significance says nothing at all about
causality. A significant correlation still has to clear all four
hurdles. The model example is
levitt on capital punishment. Even accepting the most generous
deterrence estimates, executions explain
about 1.5% of the 1990s homicide decline. Possibly real.
Definitely not the answer.
Correlation puts a number on how tightly two variables move
together. Pearson's R runs from
negative 1 to positive 1. The sign tells you direction. The size
tells you strength. Two
cautions. An R of 0 means no straight line relationship. A
perfect U shape has an R near 0. And
R squared is the share of the veridation in Y that X accounts
for. The chocolate study had an R of 0.79,
so R squared is about 0.62, which sounds impressive and is still
not causal. Regression goes further and
gives you a prediction rule. The equation is Y equals a plus
bead X. The letter A is the intercept,
which is the predicted value of Y when X is 0. The letter bead
is the slope, and bead is the thing
you will be asked about. Here is the sentence to write on the
exam. A one unit increase in X is
associated with a change of B units in Y. Notice that I said
associated with, not causes. The slope is a
description of the data. Causality still has to clear the four
hurdles. In multiple regression,
each coefficient is the effect of that variable holding all the
other variables in the model
constant. That is what statistical control looks like in
practice, and it is why regression tables
have so many rows. Reading a regression table, each row is a
variable. The first number is the
coefficient, which gives you direction and size. Underneath or
beside it, usually in parentheses,
is the standard error, which tells you how precise the estimate
is. Asterisks or a P column tell you
significance, and here is a rule of thumb worth having. If the
coefficient is more than about
twice its standard error, it is significant at the .05 level.
Last concept unit. What do you do when
you only have a handful of cases? King, Kenohane and Verba give
you one rule that decides most of it.
Select your cases on the independent variable, never on the
dependent variable, and never on both.
Why does selecting on the dependent variable break everything?
Because if every case has the same
outcome, you have no varination in why, and no varination means
zero information. If you study
twenty civil wars to find out what causes civil wars, you can
learn nothing, because you never see the
countries that had the same conditions and stayed peaceful. Same
problem if you study only successful
startups, or only school shooters. There is a subtler version.
If you keep only the high end of why,
not all of it, you do not get zero information, you get a bias
to estimate. Specifically, truncating
on Y biases the estimated effect toward zero, it makes X look
weaker than it really is. There is one
consolation. Because the direction of the bias is known, a
significant effect found in a truncated
sample means the true effect is at least that large. Selecting
on both X and Y is the worst case,
the bias can run in any direction and you cannot know which. And
here is the trap. Any selection
rule that is correlated with Y creates this bias, even one you
never thought of as selecting on Y.
Using only cases covered in newspapers. Only important cases.
Only cases where data happens
to be available. Only organizations that survived long enough to
study. Selecting on X, by contrast,
is fine. Deliberately picking cases with very different values
of X actually increases your
leverage. The only cost is that your findings apply to that
range of X. One more note. Random
selection is the default for large samples, but it is risky with
small ones. With six cases,
a random draw can easily be unrepresentative. That is why King,
Kilohane and Verber recommend
intentional selection on X for qualitative work. The
Frickonomics chapter on drug dealers pairs with
this. Sadir Venkadish got a crack gang's actual financial
records, which showed foot soldiers
earning below minimum wage, while the leader took a large share.
What one gang's books can do is show
a mechanism and kill a stereotype. What they cannot do is
establish a general causal claim. One non-randomly
obtained case. No comparison group. No variation in the outcome.
Now let me run the seven debates
quickly. For each one. The claim. The test. The verdict. Debate
one. What's the matter with Kansas?
Claim. Thomas Frank says working class whites vote against their
economic interests because of culture.
Test. Bartels. Using 14 elections of American National Election
Studies survey data, with region
and income controlled. Verdict. It does not survive. Minus 5.9
overall. Minus 19.7 in the South. Minus 1.0 outside
it, and plus 4.5 among the poorest whites. Economic issues
outweighed abortion in vote choice by more
than 2 to 1. Methods lessen. Operationalization decides the
answer. Debate two. Who receives public
assistance? Claim. Americans oppose welfare because of how they
picture the poor, and the picture is
racialized. Test. Martin Jilins uses content analysis. He codes
the racial composition of poor
people shown in news magazine photographs and network television
coverage, and compares it to the
actual composition of the poor and census data. Verdict. The
media portrait is systematically
unrepresentative, and public misperception tracks the portrait
rather than the data. Methods lessen.
Content analysis as a measurement strategy, and comparing a
measured perception against a measured
renality. Debate three. Is stop and frisk racial profiling?
Claim. Michael Bloomberg argues that stop
rates should be benchmarked against descriptions of criminal
suspects, not against the population,
so the racial disparity is not profiling. Test. Bertrand and
Molinathan stop arguing about the
right denominator and randomly assign race to otherwise
identical resumes. Verdict. 9.65% versus
6.45%. Methods lessen. The entire op-ed fight is about choosing
a comparison group, and an experiment
builds the comparison group by construction. Debate four. Does
money buy votes? Claim.
Contributions correlate with roll call votes. They're for donors
by legislators. Test. John Wright points
out that this is a weak design, because donors give to
legislators who already agree, so causation may
run backwards. Then Hertel Fernandez and colleagues survey 101
senior congressional staffers and compare
their beliefs about constituent opinion against actual
estimates. Verdict. Staffers misjudge their
constituents badly and in a conservative direction. 91%
underestimated support for gun background checks.
78% underestimated support for limits on carbon dioxide. And a
list experiment found that 45% had
developed a new perspective after talking with a group that made
campaign contributions.
The channel is not buying votes. It is shaping what legislators
believe voters want. Methods lessen.
Reverse causation. And the list experiment has a way to ask an
embarrassing question.
Debate five. Who votes? And is it getting worse? Claim. Turnout
is falling, and as inequality grows,
then electorate is getting richer relative to the country. Test.
Lili and Nagler. Current population
survey data from 1972 to 2008. Using representativeness ratios
and relative measures. Verdict. Both claims
fail. Methods lessen. Denominators change conclusions. And
relative measures beat absolute ones when you
compare across decades. Debate six. Are independents rising?
Claim. A record 40% of Americans call
themselves independent, so they are the largest and most
decisive block in politics. Test. Keith and
colleagues push independence on which party they lean toward.
Then Fowler and colleagues model more than
280,000 survey respondents' actual positions across 20-plus
policy questions, instead of trusting a
self-applied label. Verdict. Most so-called independents are
closet partisans who lean and
then vote that way. Alan Abramowitz puts genuinely uncommitted
voters at less than 10% of actual voters.
And Fowler finds that about 73% of Americans are well described
by a single left-right dimension,
21% hold genuine but idiosyncratic views, and 6.5% are simply
answering inattentively.
Here is the kicker. Inattentive respondents give more extreme
answers than actual extremists do.
Methods lessen. A self-reported label is not the concept, and
measurement error can masquerade as
a real category. Debate seven. Why did crime fall in the 1990s?
Claim. Malcolm Gladwell says crime
behaves like an epidemic with a tipping point. And broken
windows policing tip New York. Test.
Stephen Levitt takes the best-identified estimate for each
proposed cause and multiplies it by how much
that factor actually changed. Robert Sampson and Alex Winter
follow a Chicago birth cohort for 18 years
to test the childhood lead hypothesis. Verdict. Homicide fell 43
% nationally, everywhere. Not just
in New York. San Diego fell 72.8%. Austin fell 69.5%. San
Jose fell 69.2%. New York fell 73.6%.
And New York hired police at three times the national rate.
Methods lessen. Effect size accounting.
And the fact that a mechanism story is not a test. Levitt's
accounting is worth memorizing and outline.
Four factors explain the decline. The rising prison population,
about 12%. Legalized abortion, about 10%.
The receding crack epidemic, about 6. And more police officers,
about 5.5. Together roughly 36 points of the
43-point drop. And six factors that do not explain it. Increased
capital punishment, about 1.5%. Innovative
policing strategies, about 1%. And the strong economy, changing
demographics, gun control laws and concealed
carry laws, all essentially zero. Now compare that to what the
10 largest newspapers actually wrote about
over the same decade. Innovative policing was mentioned 52
times. Prisons, 47. The strong economy,
28. And legalized abortion. Levitt's second largest factor was
mentioned zero times. Copular explanations get
ranked by how satisfying they are, not by how much they explain.
Let me close with what the exams actually
look like. Professor Trounstein's stated goal is that you can
analyze, explain and apply your knowledge to
new and different contexts. So expect an unfamiliar claim and a
request to evaluate it. Five frames cover
most of it. Frame 1. Here is a claim from the news. Evaluate it.
Run the four hurdles in order. Say yes,
no or maybe to each, with a reason. Name the specific confounder
you are worried about, not just other factors.
Then finish by saying what evidence would settle it. Usually
that is an experiment that randomly assigned
x. And then you explain why that is impossible here and what the
next best design would be.
Frame 2. Design a study to answer this question. Date the
hypothesis with a direction. Name the unit
of analysis. Give an operational definition for x and for y, and
defend it against a validity objection.
Say how you would assign or approximate assigning x. Name your
control group and say what makes it
a credible counterfactual. Then admit the biggest remaining
threat to internal validity. Frame 3.
Why is this measure bad? Separate validity from reliability.
Then say which direction the error
runs, because systematic error is far worse than random noise.
Frame 4. This poll says x. How much
should you trust it? Sampling error is the smallest error
present. Ask about the frame, the response rate,
the waiting, and the likely voter screen. Cite Cohn or cite
Clinton. Recommend averaging polls,
and note that averaging does not fix house effects. Frame 5.
Interpret this table or coefficient.
Say the direction, the size and real units, and whether it is
significant, using the rule that the
coefficient should be more than twice its standard error. Then
say what it does not tell you. In a
multiple regression, always add the phrase holding the other
variables constant, and never write causes
unless the design earns it. That is the course. If you take one
thing from this recording, take the four
hurdles, in order, mechanism, reverse causation, coveration,
confounders. If you take two things, take the four
hurdles and the difference between random assignment and random
sampling. And if you have five minutes
before a quiz, run the seven debates in your head. Plame, test,
verdict, Kansas, welfare, profiling, money,
turn out, independence, crime. Good luck.
